news.title: Goldman hikes oil-price forecasts on ‘substantial’ supply risks
news.text:
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. raised oil-price forecasts for the year-end and 2027 on elevated risks to supplies, joining other banks in hiking their outlooks after months of war in the Middle East.

Brent is now seen at $105 a barrel in December, up from a previous estimate of $90, and will average $88 next year, 10 per cent more than seen before, analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby said in a note, which also increased forecasts for US oil marker West Texas Intermediate. 

“Substantial downside supply risks are likely to sustain a large, near-term risk premium,” the analysts wrote. The markets are assigning “increasing weight to escalation after the Nov. 3 US midterms and subsequent potential weakness in Mideast supply,” they added in the Nov. 1 report.

Global benchmark Brent rallied 14 per cent in October, hitting a six-month high, even as crude supplies from the Middle East rebounded close to pre-war levels. The gains came on concern that hostilities between the US and Iran may flare up again after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump repeatedly hinting that he may resume airstrikes. For his part, Iran’s Supreme Leader has ordered his top commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation. 

Intensified shipping attacks and damage to infrastructure were among factors that could trigger further price gains, the analysts said, while also highlighting risks from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “With the timing and location of disruptions nearly impossible to predict, our base case now includes a 1-million-barrel-per-day global supply disruption allowance in 2027.”

In recent weeks, Morgan Stanley raised its forecast for Dated Brent — a key physical price — to $105 a barrel for the fourth quarter, while ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. hiked its year-end outlook for Brent futures to the same figure. Most-active contracts last traded near $110 after dropping in Monday’s trade.

More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com

Published on November 2, 2026
news.summary: Brent is now seen at $105 a barrel in December, up from a previous estimate of $90, and will average $88 next year, 10% more than seen before

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed's Appeal to Michiganders After Haley Stevens' Sudden Switch
news.text: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday night that he understood some Detroit residents might have reservations about him based on their experiences with people who look like him, adding that he wanted to be judged on his character. Speaking with MS NOW in the hours after former Democratic rival Haley Stevens switched her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed said he felt he had been consistent in his message as he seeks to win Michigan's open, Democratic-held U.S. Senate seat. Democrats need to take back control of the chamber. El-Sayed has been a frequent target of Republican criticism, including attacks on his Muslim faith and attempts to portray his political views as extremist. "I know that for too many people in the city of Detroit, their interactions with people who look like me aren't very good," El-Sayed said. "They're being catcalled behind bulletproof glass in the gas station or a liquor store, watching kids get sold loosie cigarettes. "But I'm asking to be judged by the content of my character, not the color of my skin, and I hope that in the U.S. Senate, I can be somebody who brings communities together so that we can build together what we can't have alone." Stevens, who currently serves in the House of Representatives, insisted that her decision to endorse Rogers was "not anti-Muslim at all" as she spoke outside a Detroit church Sunday. She and El-Sayed have publicly differed in their view on Israel's military campaign in Gaza. Gaza health authorities say the campaign has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers' campaigns for comment via email outside of normal working hours Sunday. Michigan's Muslim Population: What to Know Michigan has one of the largest Muslim populations in the U.S., with an estimated 241,828 Muslim adherents, equivalent to about 2.4 percent of the state's population, according to the 2020 U.S. Religion Census. The U.S. Census does not ask Americans about their religion. The state's Muslim population, as well as its Arab American and Middle Eastern communities, are largely concentrated around Wayne County and the metro Detroit area, particularly in Dearborn, which became a focal point of the 2024 presidential election. The city's 2020 census data showed 54.5 percent of residents identifying as having Middle Eastern or North African ancestry. The communities grew over a significant period of time, including Arab migration to support Michigan's auto industry in the early 20th century, and later waves from Iraq, Yemen, and elsewhere in the Middle East. In 2020, President Joe Biden won Dearborn with 68.8 percent of the vote, compared with 29.9 percent for President Donald Trump. Trump's first administration had imposed travel restrictions on several predominantly Muslim countries, an issue that contributed to opposition among some Arab American voters. In 2022, Democrats won the Michigan governorship and control of both chambers of the state Legislature. In Dearborn, protests over LGBTQ+-themed school library books became a political flashpoint, with some conservative Muslim residents and Republicans calling for their removal. Democrats Rashida Tlaib and Alabas Farhat, who represented Dearborn in Congress and the state House, respectively, both won re-election. The 2024 election saw a major shift, with Trump winning across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights, while former Vice President Kamala Harris won in Hamtramck. Opposition to the Biden administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza played a major role in the shift away from Democrats among Muslim voters, according to a 2024 exit poll by the Council on American-Islamic Relations. El-Sayed and other Muslim Americans running for or serving in elected offices have faced pushback for their views on Israel. The Democratic Senate candidate has described Israel's conduct in Gaza as a genocide and said he does not support U.S. military assistance to Israel. Some Jewish organizations and political opponents have criticized his positions on Israel, but El-Sayed has condemned antisemitism and Hamas, while arguing that criticism of Israel and its military campaign should not be equated with hostility toward Jewish people. El-Sayed's Response to Stevens' Switch Earlier Sunday, despite saying in recent days she was still backing El-Sayed, Stevens said she was switching her vote to Rogers, while still remaining a staunch Democrat. The move sparked criticism from several Democrats, as well as strategists and commentators. El-Sayed said he was not worried about Stevens and rather the other 9.9 million in the state who were not her. "Mike Rogers is going to be a vote for Donald Trump," he told MS NOW. "And if you don't believe me, just ask Donald Trump. He came here last Sunday and said that he is on the ballot. In fact, he is on the ballot in the form of Mike Rogers, and so I'm asking folks to say, what are your priorities? "If there are issues that we disagree on that are more important to you than protecting democracy, protecting the right to choose, protecting the right to a union, protecting health care, then so be it," El-Sayed said. "But if you believe in defending our democracy, defending health care, defending the insane attack on our policies, our politics, frankly, our democracy, then I hope that I can earn your support." Stevens appeared on CNN around an hour after El-Sayed's MS NOW appearance, with Anderson Cooper asking her if she believed her fellow Democrat was spreading hate or antisemitism, which she had said she could not stand alongside. "I think some of the actions have certainly been antisemitic, Anderson, but I am just sick of who he stands with," Stevens said. Trump praised Stevens' decision, telling reporters in Iowa he would like to see her join the GOP. He also took to Truth Social to praise the Congresswoman. "Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," Trump wrote. "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did. It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!" Stevens told CNN she wanted to see Democrats hold Trump accountable, with Cooper asking her if she wanted her party to win control of the Senate. "I absolutely do," she said. "I'm just casting my vote this one way." Cooper said she was not just casting her vote; she was "very publicly" casting it. Stevens was asked repeatedly what had changed between late Saturday, when she was reported to have said she was still supporting El-Sayed, and Sunday morning's announcement. She did not appear to answer the question, instead repeating El-Sayed had become "angrier and angrier." El-Sayed Remains Ahead in Final Polls To win control of the Senate, Democrats need to retain all their current seats, including the open Michigan seat, and flip at least four others, with eyes on Texas, Maine, Ohio, and Kansas. On Sunday, the final poll before Election Day from The New York Times/Siena was released, showing El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Rogers, at 53 percent compared to 42 percent among 1,011 likely voters conducted October 23-November 1. A previous poll, from YouGov, conducted October 26-29 among 2,093 voters, had El-Sayed with a 4-point lead of 51 percent to 47 percent. El-Sayed has largely been ahead in polling since early September, barring two polls affiliated with Republican sponsors. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steven Frank.
news.summary: The Democratic U.S. Senate candidate saw his polling take an 11-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers Sunday.
news.author: Dan Gooding

news.title: US Congressman refuses to rule out Trump impeachment if Democrats win House
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 2 (IANS) US Congressman and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has declined to rule out impeaching President Donald Trump if Democrats win control of the House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterm elections, saying his party's focus remains on the cost of living. Asked by ABC News whether impeachment would be a distraction from the work Democrats are trying to do, Jeffries said: "Well, we haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out because we've made it clear that we are focused on addressing the affordability crisis." "We believe that it is important for Congress to function as a check and balance on an out-of-control Executive Branch," the New York Democrat said in the interview, which was aired on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday. ABC News Capitol Hill correspondent Jay O'Brien, who spoke to Jeffries on the campaign trail days earlier, said Jeffries had described his day-one priorities as the cost of living, "in particular, health care and rising gas and grocery prices." According to O'Brien, Democrats are "not just running on affordability, but accountability, too," and are promising a string of investigations into Trump and his administration if they return to power. He reported that some subpoenas were already being prepared, with investigative steps aimed at the President, his administration, his family's businesses and its cryptocurrency interests. The White House has consistently denied any conflicts of interest, ABC News reported. O'Brien also noted that several House Democrats had openly talked in recent months about impeaching Trump for a third time. Trump was impeached twice by the Democratic-led House during his first term and was acquitted by the Senate both times. A House impeachment requires only a simple majority, but removal from office would need a two-thirds vote, or 67 votes, in the Senate. If Democrats win the House, Jeffries is poised to become the first Black Speaker in American history, O'Brien said. ABC News also reported that it had spoken to House Speaker Mike Johnson, who said he was confident Republicans would defy the polls and history. Asked whether a Republican defeat would be a message from voters seeking change, Johnson said he would not view it as a message, but as a sign that voters were misinformed, according to O'Brien's account. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to win the House majority. Election forecasters rate them as favourites to do so, while the battle for the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 of the 100 seats, is seen as closer. Polls close across the country on Tuesday night.

news.title: Dozens of Commonwealth leaders descend on Antigua during global political turbulence
news.text:
Leaders representing nearly a third of the world’s population are meeting on the tiny Caribbean island of Antigua this week to strengthen ties during a time of global political upheaval.

New deals and pledges are expected to emerge from the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, which is held every two years. More than 50 leaders of Commonwealth nations, many of which once formed part of the British Empire, are scheduled to attend, along with officials from Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates.

“To deal with what to expect in Antigua, I think we need … to look at the world in which we find ourselves today,” Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey told The Associated Press ahead of the meeting. “We’re looking at issues like conflict, economic shocks, rising costs, climate change, trade, weaponization of tariffs; and all of this hitting directly the pockets of our people.”

Botchwey said Commonwealth leaders representing 2.7 billion people will look at how to attract investment and reduce barriers to intra-Commonwealth trade.

“For us, this is extremely important,” she said. “All the countries woke up one day and were slapped with tariffs. If we are trading more among ourselves, whatever happens outside the Commonwealth will not affect countries too much.”

U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression, although rates have fluctuated amid legal challenges.

Botchwey said that creating stronger economies is essential given the trade wars: “It’s an opportunity we cannot miss.”

The Commonwealth of Nations also seeks to create a fund to provide digital skills to about 10 million young adults, she said, adding that she hopes the private sector, foundations and philanthropies will contribute.

Officials are also expected to establish a fund to help nations transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.

Climate will be a big talking point because 49 of the Commonwealth’s 56 countries share a border with the ocean as concerns grow over rising sea levels.

“How are we going to prepare them and ensure that our ocean is healthy?” Botchwey said.

The four-day meeting also will host forums focusing on business, women and young people.

Richardo Aiken, a civil society governor who represents the Caribbean and Americas at the Commonwealth Foundation, said in a phone interview that climate justice, freedom of expression and empowering vulnerable groups will likely dominate the people’s forum in Antigua.

“We also have a large population of Indigenous people,” he said. “It’s about how do we bring these players, the first people, those who were before us, into the conversation?”

He expects the forum to propose specific initiatives to help civil organizations overcome various barriers, including not knowing how to write proposals, “which is the main vehicle to access financing.”

Climate change also will dominate conversations, Aiken said.

“We are actually living in one of the most vulnerable regions in the world,” he said.

Some Caribbean leaders also have called for slavery reparations to be discussed at the four-day meeting, which King Charles III is expected to attend after visiting the Bahamas and Guyana last week. Queen Camilla is expected to join him.

The meeting’s opening ceremony is slated for Tuesday morning, and the event is scheduled to end on Wednesday.
news.summary: Leaders representing nearly a third of the world’s population are meeting on the tiny Caribbean island of Antigua this week to strengthen ties during a time of global political upheaval
news.author: Danica Coto

news.title: Binance sees outflows stabilising as exchange returns online after $6.3 billion heist
news.text: Customers withdrew $3.64 billion, flows 'stabilising' now Binance covers 95% of $6.3 billion in stolen tokens FBI and analysts say North Korea behind attack but Trump says US not certain Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1 per cent of its assets, as the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion ‌stolen from the platform last week. The exchange moved to reassure crypto investors and said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial ​spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial" after, what analysts believe, may be the world's biggest financial robbery ever. After hitting ⁠a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday. Ether hit a two-month low on Friday and also recovered a little to $2,287. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally. It said on Sunday it had $171 billion ‌in total assets under management as of October 28. The Binance theft adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs. Withdrawal levels are an early ‌test of whether customers still trust Binance with their money after the attack. The exchange said it had covered 95 per cent of the ‌assets ⁠stolen in the heist. Stablecoin market capitalisations tend to fall when money is leaving cryptocurrencies and they have dropped since Friday. ⁠The combined capitalisation of the two largest stablecoins, USDT and USDC, has dropped by about $1.2 billion since Friday, according to Coinmarketcap.com. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed $643 million on Friday, the largest daily outflow of October, and more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs. "I get why, for ​conservative institutional investors, this is unsettling," Redbord said. "A hack at ‌a financial institution means stolen usernames and passwords. A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital." PHASED WITHDRAWALS Binance said on Sunday it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using its money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5 per cent of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may ‌take longer to source, it said. Despite those measures, some users were weighing options to hedge risks. Jay Koh, vice president at ​the Asia Web3 AI Association, said he had not withdrawn any of his holdings from Binance, as most of his funds were held in a cold wallet, which was not impacted by the hack. "I would not necessarily withdraw ⁠everything from Binance ... However, I do think it is prudent to review exposure, diversify custody arrangements and avoid keeping more assets on any single platform than necessary." Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in stages, prioritising user demand. The first phase ‌covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin. "We are taking a phased approach by prioritising tokens based on the past week data of user demand," Binance said in an earlier article posted on X. It added, "Rest assured that market conditions are stable." Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited after the event. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $5.81 billion, up from the $4.36 billion it showed earlier. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updated figures. "This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our ‌last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted)," a spokesperson for Binance said of the initial DefiLlama data. FBI ​TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. ⁠Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the ⁠cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Analysts had also pointed to North Korea's involvement. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on ‌Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. US President Donald Trump, however, later on Saturday said it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved. "We don't know if it's North Korea — ​but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters in comments posted by a White House account on X. (Reporting by Rae Wee in Singapore; Writing by Scott Murdoch; Editing by Sonali Paul) Customers withdrew $3.64 billion, flows 'stabilising' now Binance covers 95% of $6.3 billion in stolen tokens FBI and analysts say North Korea behind attack but Trump says US not certain
news.summary: After hitting ⁠a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Trump ends midterm campaign in Kansas, says US can 'close down' Iran 'any time'
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 2 (IANS) US President Donald Trump wrapped up his midterm campaign at a rally in Salina, Kansas, telling supporters the United States could shut Iran down whenever it chose and claiming that no one had entered the country illegally for 17 months. "This is actually, this is our last stop. We close it down tonight," Trump said, describing the Salina event as his 30th rally of the campaign. He said he had come to Kansas to help Senator Roger Marshall win re-election. "I didn't want to take a chance," he said. The rally went ahead after Trump had earlier this week called off in-person events in Kansas and Iowa in favour of tele-rallies. He spoke in Iowa earlier on Sunday before flying to Kansas. On Iran, Trump said the US had overwhelmed Tehran. "We can we can close them down any time we want. We're trying to be nice," he said. "But I think it's going to be very close. We're just going to close them down. That's going to be the end of it." He contrasted his approach with the 2015 nuclear deal signed under former President Barack Obama. "You know, that JCPOA was a path to a nuclear weapon. We did the opposite," Trump said, adding that Iran "never will have a nuclear weapon." Trump also said US oil prices were "much lower than Sleepy Joe Biden and Barack Hussein Obama." US Energy Information Administration figures show the national average price of regular gasoline at about $4.27 a gallon on October 26, about $1.23 higher than a year earlier, while West Texas Intermediate crude averaged about $107 a barrel in the week ended October 23, compared with about $73 to $79 a barrel in January 2025, when Biden left office. On immigration, Trump repeated a claim that the southern border had been sealed. "And now we've gone 17 months, think of it, with zero people coming into our country illegally," he said. He said Democrats were "openly promising to abolish your borders" and accused them of wanting to "raise your taxes by trillions and trillions of dollars." Much of the speech targeted Marshall's Democratic opponent, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, whom Trump called "a radical left lunatic." He also urged voters to back Republican Ty Masterson for governor. Trump urged supporters to vote in person on Tuesday rather than mail in ballots. "I really want you to pretend I'm on the ballot," he said, adding that if Republicans matched turnout from his own elections, "we win in a landslide."

news.title: Iran defines vast arena to inflict damage on enemy: IRGC spokesman
news.text: Digital Desk | Tehran, Nov 2 (IANS) Iranian forces have determined a vast battlefield to inflict damage on the "enemy" and achieve complete deterrence, spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Hossein Mohebbi has said. Speaking at a conference in Iran's southeastern Kerman province on Sunday (local time), Mohebbi said Iranian forces are more prepared than ever "to respond decisively to the enemy," reports Xinhua, quoting the semi-official Tasnim news agency. He pointed to recent orders from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to senior military commanders, saying the leader's guidelines "opened a new chapter of war." Mohebbi highlighted Khamenei's emphasis that "there is no geographical limitation in the war with the United States," saying the IRGC has placed on its agenda identifying new enemy targets and planning operations in new geographical regions. On Saturday, a statement announced that Iran's supreme leader had ordered senior commanders of the armed forces to ensure that any level and kind of threat from the "enemies" must be met with an "immediate and effective" response without geographical limitations. The warnings come amid heightened US threats of military action against Iran. According to The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), US President Donald Trump was briefed on Thursday by top US military officials on options regarding Iran. The United States has also informed several Gulf countries to prepare for a possible brief but intense military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections, according to the WSJ. On February 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and US bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.

news.title: Dire warning as 'cornered and desperate' Trump ally tips the world toward nuclear war
news.text:
President Donald Trump may be "sleepwalking" toward a nuclear conflict at the urging of one of his "cornered and desperate" allies, according to one analyst. 

Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host, posted a lengthy warning on X, alleging that the Trump administration may approve a nuclear strike on Iran within a week of the midterm elections. It's an issue that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu calls Trump about "every day," according to Carlson. 

"The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program," Carlson wrote. " No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one."

Carlson noted that the recent election results in Israel made Netanyahu's pleas more urgent. Netanyahu's governing coalition took a shellacking in the election because of a surge in support for Israel's Arab parties, which could pave the way for Netanyahu's exit from state politics. 

"Netanyahu is cornered and desperate," Carlson noted. "After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations, and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war."

"No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final," Carlson added. 

"We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months," Carlson added. "Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called 'battlefield nukes' easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it."

news.title: At least 19 dead in Venezuela army attack on Colombian rebel camp
news.text: Caracas, Venezuela: At least 19 people were killed in the Venezuelan army's recent attack on a Colombian guerrilla group's camp inside Venezuela, an NGO and source close to the operation said Sunday.The FundaRedes NGO -- which monitors rights violations in Venezuela's border states -- initially reported nine deaths in the attack early Friday morning in the western state of Apure.Juan Francisco Garcia, a coordinator with the group, told AFP on Sunday that "another 10 bodies" had been transported to the state capital San Fernando the day after the attack.The attack targeted a camp of the National Liberation Army, a Colombian guerrilla group known by its Spanish initials, ELN.Video shared by FundaRedes showed bodies lying on the ground, trees knocked down and the ruins of what appeared to be a camp site.A Venezuelan military source close to the operation, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the attack had been supported by US intelligence."We had help from the CIA and the FBI. This was an order from the United States," the source said.Requests for comment from the US State Department and Venezuelan government were not immediately answered.The strikes were carried out by drones and attack helicopters targeting the camp, which was located in a rural, forested area in the southwest of Apure, the military source said.The attack took the guerrillas by surprise -- they had no time to react, the source said, noting that most of the people killed were Venezuelan nationals. 'More camps' After the attack, bodies were initially transported to the town of Puerto Paez, which lies across a river from Colombia.."Several of the bodies were completely mangled. Even as they were being taken to San Fernando, they still smelled of burnt flesh," a resident of Puerto Paez told AFP.Several armed groups engage in drug trafficking, illegal mining and smuggling along Venezuela and Colombia's porous 2,200-kilometer (1,367-mile) border, including dissident members of the now-defunct FARC and the ELN.The ELN has been among the most powerful rebel group in Latin America since the FARC guerrilla army signed a peace accord with the Bogota government in 2016.The military operation along the border may represent the latest shift in Venezuelan policy since the US ouster of Nicolas Maduro in January.Venezuela's government has since been led by Delcy Rodriguez, Maduro's former deputy who has won vocal support from US President Donald Trump for bending to his administration's demands.Colombia has for years accused Venezuela's leftist government of turning a blind eye to Colombian rebel groups in border areas.Human rights advocate and military affairs expert Rocio San Miguel said the Friday attack reflects a "change in doctrine" within the Venezuelan military.The military source told AFP that Venezuelan forces were "going to continue combing through the area because we believe there are more camps."The operation also comes as Colombia's newly elected hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, ramps up a violent crackdown on the ELN and drug trafficking groups in his country.Colombia has joined over a dozen other Latin American and Caribbean nations in a US-led regional effort to combat drug trafficking and organized crime across the region..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: A Cold War blueprint for today’s nuclear dangers
news.text: For reasons that could range from good to atrocious, U.S. President Donald Trump wants a three-way summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts when the three men are in Shenzhen next month for an economic forum.In the worst scenario, Trump and Xi Jinping would conspire to doom Ukraine to Vladimir Putin’s subjugation. In the best, however, they would open a long and necessary process toward an eventual nuclear detente among the U.S., Russia and China. Trump claims he wants this trilateral meeting “not so much for Ukraine” but “to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization.” Let’s take him at his word.What would such talks look like? And what lesson could Trump take from a West German chancellor in the 1970s?
news.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump wants a three-way summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization.

news.title: Private plane carrying nine aboard crashes in Florida and erupts in massive fireball
news.text:
At least nine people are dead after a plane crashed in Florida’s Palm Beach County on Sunday and erupted into a big fireball.

The Learjet 60 went down in a neighborhood near Cresthaven in South Florida at 12:50 p.m. All nine people onboard the business jet were killed, according to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The Bahamas-bound flight had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas.

“Today's plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy,” Duffy wrote. 

“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost — Federal Aviation Administration & U.S. Department of Transportation are closely monitoring this crash and will share updates as we learn more.”

It wasn’t immediately clear if anyone on the ground was injured or what caused the jet to crash.

Teams with the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration were headed to the scene, located near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North.

 The crash site is located roughly eight miles from President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate. Trump was in Iowa for a midterms election rally around the time of the crash.

Jim Reynolds, spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the plane was a private aircraft with tail number N722BD but he could not yet provide details about who was onboard.

“This is definitely a tragedy,” he said.

Video captured by witnesses inside their cars showed the aircraft nose-diving from the sky and exploding into a giant ball of flames on a major road, inches from passing cars. 

The crash left a huge crater in the pavement, with flames seen leaping up near a roadside utility pole.

Chunks of pavement were engulfed in flames as people stood nearby, expressing shock that it landed feet from homes. Black smoke billowed out of the hole in the ground.

It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.

news.title: Trump Met by Taunts and Jeers on Final Campaign Stretch
news.text:
President Donald Trump has been met by a public display of taunts, jeers and NSFW protest signs on his final campaign stretch.

Trump, 80, visited Dubuque, Iowa on Sunday, ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election. The appearance came as the senior president reversed his initial decision to cancel the trip on Thursday, stating he would appear via telerally.

The about-face gave anti-Trump demonstrators the chance to share their thoughts with the president in person.

As the presidential motorcade passed through the streets on the way to the rally venue at the Five Flags Civic Center, a string of protesters held up signs and made obscene gestures at Trump, according to pictures captured by Reuters and Getty photographers.

One NSFW sign read, “2 Days A-----e,” referring to the date of the midterm election, while multiple people were photographed flipping Trump the bird.

Signs waved at the president included, “Trump Do Better,” “Jail The Pedos,” and “The Only Orange Monarch I Want is a Butterfly.”

Others included “The World’s a Trumpster Fire,” “Trump Epstein Files Coming Soon!,” and “Guardian of the Pedophiles.”

Some protesters shouted at people attending the rally as they entered the venues, the Des Moines Register reported, and noted signs that read “This Regime Doesn’t Care About You,” and “Elect a Clown, Expect a Circus.”

Other signs called for Trump’s impeachment and an end to his war with Iran, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch, noting that Republican candidate Ashley Hinson asked the crowd at the rally to stand and chant “U.S.A” so the protesters outside could hear.

The protests followed a report that the Trump administration had attempted to make Dubuque more welcoming to the president.

Trump’s team wanted to shield a racial solidarity mural on the city-owned Five Flags Civic Center, according to the Des Moines Register.

On Saturday, social media users highlighted a tarp being placed over Dubuque artist Shelby Fry’s “Solidarity” mural. Late on Saturday, the city released a statement saying that it was not asked if the exterior of the Five Flags Civic Center “could be modified and did not authorize the tarp.”

The mural, which is 105 feet long and 28 feet wide, depicts 10 raised Black, brown and White fists, with a letter on each to spell out the word “SOLIDARITY.” It has been in place on the side of the building since 2020. 

The letters also include a Pride rainbow and emblems for disability rights, mental health and gender diversity, all triggers for the Trump administration.

The White House had wanted to erect a U.S. flag on the building instead, according to KCRG-TV.

The anti-Trump sentiment also continued inside the venue, during his near-two-hour speech. The Des Moines Register said protesters inside were chanted down and escorted out of the venue three times.

The interruptions have become a fixture at Trump’s rallies this month, and he repeated his usual disclaimer in Dubuque, claiming, “They’re paid protesters, they go away quickly. They’re like a gnat, they’re like a little fly.”

He continued, “There’s usually two or three of them per rally,” claiming they get paid $250.

Trump seemed to lose his temper after being shouted for a third time during his Iowa rally, barking “You’re a stupid person!”

Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek is beating Trump-endorsed Ashley Hinson for the seat of outgoing GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in Iowa in a close Senate race, with a MS NOW poll stating Turek is on 47.1 percent to Hinson on 46.5 percent.

Trump’s second rally for Sunday is due to happen in Salina, Kansas. The White House has announced Trump will make his closing pitch at the midterms at his problematic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

news.title: Trump says ‘at some point’ US will have to give Iran ‘the hammer’
news.text:
DUBUQUE, Iowa: US President Donald Trump has renewed his threat to launch military strikes against Iran, saying Washington may eventually have to “give them the hammer,” as Tehran warned that any renewed conflict could last longer than the previous round of fighting.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, a day before the US midterm elections, Trump said he had held back from further attacks because he wanted to avoid additional casualties.

“The only reason why I'm not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he told supporters. “But at some point we're going to have to give them the hammer.”

Trump had earlier told reporters that Washington still needed to deal with one or two remaining targets in Iran, suggesting they could be struck within minutes. He specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected underground nuclear complex.

His latest remarks came amid uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to prevent a resumption of the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began on Feb. 28.

US media reported that Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday about negotiations with Tehran and the possibility of escalating military operations. Axios reported that Netanyahu was pressing for an immediate strike after the US midterm elections, while Trump wanted to give diplomacy more time.

‘No geographical limitations’

Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned that another war could last longer than the previous conflict, saying Washington would not be able to dictate its timing or terms.

Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi echoed the warning, saying there would be “no geographical limitations” to the battlefield in a confrontation with Washington.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran remained prepared for both diplomacy and defense, expressing hope that Washington would choose negotiations.

Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks, although Tehran had yet to respond.

Iran has demanded the release of frozen assets, an end to the US naval blockade of its ports, sanctions relief and a comprehensive end to the fighting. The Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route, remains a major point of contention.

‘Braced for the worst’

Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, said the Emirates hoped diplomatic efforts would produce a breakthrough but was preparing for renewed fighting.

“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round,” he told a conference in Manama, adding that the UAE was “braced for the worst.”

news.text:
President Donald Trump’s anatomical analysis of his female Senate pick was cut short by an anti-MAGA protester.

A protester interrupted the 80-year-old president mid-tangent as he described how his Iowa Senate pick, Rep. Ashley Hinson, used to be “a little bit heavier.”

“I knew Ashley for a long time, and she was a little bit heavier, okay?” Trump said at his rally in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. “She was. And she put herself—she knew what she was doing. She knew the weight that was on her—really, literally, the weight.”

“And she knew the importance of what she was doing, and she went out—the old-fashioned way, too. Not with, you know, give me a shot,” he rambled on, referring to GLP-1 drugs.

As he was about to deliver his “punchline,” a demonstrator interrupted the president’s speech—a common occurrence throughout his last-minute midterm panic tour. Trump was not happy.

“Oh, don’t bother. They’re paid protesters, don’t worry. They go away quickly,” he said, prompting a “USA” chant from the crowd. “They’re like a gnat. They’re like a little fly.”

He continued after about a 15-second pause, “There’s usually two or three of them per rally. They get paid $250. They’re paid by [George] Soros. And they’re losers.”

“But they always do it right in the middle of my punchline!” he yelled, before returning to his analysis of his candidate’s weight. “Because I was about to say that Ashley knew the importance of what this was and how important it was, and boy, she put herself—she went on a regimen, she put herself in shape. She’s in perfect shape.”

He concluded, “I thought she was great the other way, but she put herself in shape, and she did that for you. She knew the importance, and I think it’s great.”

Not long after commenting on her weight, Trump welcomed Hinson to the stage with an awkward cheek kiss.

The Daily Beast reached out to the White House and Hinson’s reps for comment.

Rather than focusing on issues affecting Americans, Trump has treated his nationwide panic tour more as a testing ground for new rant material, much of which has focused on his obsession with people’s appearances.

At several rallies over the past few weeks, the president has repeatedly waxed poetic about Ohio incumbent Sen. Jon Husted’s “a--,” prompting bipartisan confusion over why he continually belabors variations of the same bizarre anecdote.

news.title: Dismay after Haley Stevens' 'absolute train wreck' CNN interview: 'What is this?'
news.text:
Onlookers were dismayed Sunday after Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) gave one of the most bizarre interviews to Anderson Cooper of CNN. 

Stevens was interviewed Sunday on CNN's "Midterms 2026: Countdown to Election Night," where Cooper asked her why she abruptly changed her mind from supporting Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed to endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump's. Stevens claimed earlier in the day that El-Sayed had effectively banished her from his campaign after she endorsed him, and that was at least part of the reason why she decided to support Rogers. 

Things got even stranger during her appearance on CNN. At one point, Stevens told Cooper that El-Sayed had gotten "angrier" throughout his campaign, a claim that Cooper didn't buy. 

"He didn't get angrier between midnight last night and this morning," Cooper said. "So, was there something specific that changed your mind?"

"Anderson, you certainly weren't on the phone with me at midnight," Stevens stammered. "And I don't think I was on the phone either."

Cooper also challenged Stevens on a claim she made at a press conference with Rogers earlier in the day. 

"You said you can't stand with hate. Do you think El-Sayed is hateful or an antisemite?" Cooper asked. 

Stevens took a swig from a water bottle that was sitting just off camera before she answered.

"I think some of the actions have certainly been antisemitic... and I'm just sick of who he stands with," Stevens said. 

Stevens' wild interview sparked a firestorm of reactions on social media. 

Journalist Aaron Rupar expressed concern for Stevens in multiple posts on X. 

"My god, Haley Stevens is an absolute train wreck. What is this?" Rupar wrote in one post, adding in another that it was "One of the most bizarre and incoherent political interviews" he had ever seen. 

Political commentator Keith Olbermann was left with just one question after the interview concluded.

"How many times can someone end their career in one 24-hour stretch?" he posted on X. 

Tahra Hoops, senior director of economic analysis at the Chamber of Progress, noted that the interview didn't help Stevens in the least. 

"Holy heck, this is bad. Painfully obvious that her entire team left her as she was NOT prepared for this," she posted on X.

news.title: US explores route to bring Russian gas back to Europe through Ukraine: Report
news.text: The US is exploring a plan to bring Russian natural gas back into the European market through pipelines crossing Ukraine, in a bid to secure an energy truce between Moscow and Kyiv before winter. The proposal is part of wider efforts to advance peace negotiations, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing officials from the US, Europe and Ukraine.The arrangement could see a US intermediary handle the sale of Russian gas, potentially bypassing European sanctions while giving American investors a stake in the business. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the proposal during their visits to Moscow and Kyiv in September, people familiar with the discussions told the WSJ.The idea faces a major obstacle: Europe's stated policy of ending its reliance on Russian energy. EU legislation requires member states to phase out all Russian natural gas purchases by the end of 2027. Several European leaders have also ruled out returning to dependence on supplies from a country they consider a major security threat.Yet Washington believes the prospect of reopening a lucrative European market could persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to agree to an energy ceasefire. The proposed route would use the Soviet-era pipeline system connecting Siberia's Urengoi gas fields to Europe through Ukraine. Kyiv, in turn, could earn much-needed money from transit charges.The proposal had lost momentum last month after Ukraine halted attacks on Russian refineries following pressure from US President Donald Trump. The pause lasted nearly two weeks, even as Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure continued and Moscow began sending diesel to the US. Washington subsequently turned its attention to the possibility of negotiating a wider peace settlement.That pause is now over. Ukraine launched attacks on three major Russian refineries over three days, beginning Friday, bringing the question of an energy truce back into focus. The renewed urgency comes ahead of planned three-way talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi in mid-November. Moscow has so far resisted US efforts to secure such an arrangement, according to the WSJ.A possible financial incentive for MoscowThe White House has also discussed safeguards to prevent Russia from using gas revenues to bankroll its military campaign. Under one proposal, proceeds from European sales would be placed in an escrow account in a third-party jurisdiction, a senior US official told the WSJ.American negotiators have presented the arrangement to European governments as a way to ease energy costs at a time when the continent is preparing for winter with relatively low gas reserves. They believe access to the European market could give Putin a strong financial reason to accept a deal.The proposal would represent a dramatic shift in Trump's approach to Russian energy. During his first term, he repeatedly criticised then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel for backing the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, warning that the project would leave Germany “captive to Russia”. His administration imposed sanctions on the pipeline in late 2019.Russia's subsequent invasion of Ukraine reinforced European concerns about the risks of relying on Moscow for energy. Before the war, Russian gas accounted for 45% of Europe's supplies. That share has since fallen to 11%, with US liquefied natural gas now making up 30% of European consumption.The EU has since moved to dismantle its dependence on Russian gas, with a complete phase-out mandated by the end of 2027. Its stated position is that purchases should not resume even after a comprehensive peace agreement, much less under a temporary ceasefire that leaves Russia's war effort intact.EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen reiterated that position in an October interview with a Hungarian newspaper, which his office confirmed.“I certainly would not trust Russia. Even if there were peace tomorrow, which we all hope for,” he said.Europe's resistance faces a new energy testDespite the public opposition, the Trump administration believes economic pressures could make European governments reconsider. Some senior officials, however, have privately rejected the idea in strong terms.A senior Nordic official said buying Russian gas again would contradict everything Europe stands for. Another senior official from a large European country likened the proposal to former British leader Neville Chamberlain sacrificing Czechoslovakia to Hitler in exchange for business deals, the WSJ reported.Washington is also considering the possibility of restoring gas supplies through Nord Stream as part of a broader settlement. The US sees such an arrangement as potentially helping not only to end the Ukraine war but also to ease longstanding tensions between Moscow and America's European allies.A senior US official told the WSJ that Merkel's mistake had been to pursue the pipeline without first securing a broader security arrangement with Russia that Moscow could accept.The Nord Stream route, however, would be difficult to revive. Nord Stream 1 stopped deliveries in August 2022, while Nord Stream 2 never entered service. Both pipelines were badly damaged in underwater explosions in September 2022, which were attributed to Ukraine. Their restoration would require considerable time and the resolution of major political and regulatory obstacles.The route through Ukraine, on the other hand, offers a quicker alternative. The pipeline network connects to Slovakia and extends towards Austria and Germany. It could be brought back into operation almost immediately, as limited gas flows continued through it until January 2025, despite the ongoing war.US officials have also discussed other economic arrangements during negotiations. One proposal that could significantly lower gas prices across Europe has drawn interest from European leaders, a US official said. However, any such arrangement would be tied to a comprehensive peace deal.The energy situation could further complicate Europe's position. The conflict involving Iran has disrupted Qatari LNG shipments, leaving cargoes stranded inside the Persian Gulf. Energy prices have climbed globally despite an increase in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.According to the EU, the conflict has added 100 billion euros, or around $112 billion, to Europe's energy costs. Meanwhile, underground gas storage across the continent is about 75% full, leaving Europe on course to enter winter with reserves below the nine-year average, EU energy regulators said.The prospect of cheaper Russian supplies has also become a political issue in Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany has made restoring imports of low-cost Russian gas a central plank of its campaign ahead of the 2028 national elections.For Ukraine, the calculation could be different if renewed gas transit forms part of an agreement that protects its energy infrastructure. Diplomats told the WSJ that Kyiv's backing could make it easier for European governments to reconsider the proposal, particularly if a ceasefire prevents blackouts and a humanitarian crisis in major Ukrainian cities.A collapse of energy supplies could trigger another wave of refugees in the coming months. The risk is compounded by Ukraine's dwindling air-defence capabilities, with the US restricting supplies of Patriot interceptors amid a global shortage linked to the war on Iran.You use AI every day. news.summary: The US is exploring a plan to resume Russian natural gas supplies to Europe through Ukraine as part of efforts to secure an energy ceasefire and advance peace talks. The proposal could offer Moscow a financial incentive while providing Kyiv with transit revenue, but faces strong European opposition amid concerns over renewed dependence on Russia.

news.title: Stock selloff eases in Asian trade, oil declines: Markets wrap
news.text:
A selloff in stocks eased during early Monday trading as Asian equities fell less than their Wall Street peers and US equity futures turned higher. Oil declined.

Benchmark indexes in Japan and Australia both fell, while those in South Korea and Hong Kong gained, leaving the MSCI Asia Pacific Index down by 0.4 per cent.

This followed a Friday session where the Nasdaq 100 Index tumbled 3.5 per cent, its worst day since June, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 7.2 per cent. Futures on the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 both climbed at least 0.4 per cent Monday, pointing to a recovery when US cash markets reopen.

Elsewhere, Brent crude fell 1.5 per cent to about $111.71 a barrel following reports that US President Donald Trump wants to give diplomacy more time before deciding whether to resume strikes on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Gold climbed 0.9 per cent to around $3,910 an ounce after falling to its lowest close in more than a year on Friday. Bitcoin climbed for a third day after sinking last week when Binance Holdings revealed a record hack that rattled the crypto industry.

China’s financial regulators will hold a meeting with banks and securities firms Monday to discuss measures to support the capital market, signaling authorities’ renewed effort to halt the slump in Chinese stocks. 

Last week’s selloff in tech shares indicates investors are showing less tolerance for tech companies whose core businesses are slowing as AI spending surges.

Results from Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. fueled concerns that AI is eroding the businesses financing those investments. Traders are bracing for more volatility, with the US midterm elections this week and Nvidia Corp. earnings later in November.

“The revelation that these hyperscalers are seeing a slowdown in their core businesses means that the big payoff that everyone has been saying will come eventually is getting pushed even further down the road,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.

All three major Chinese financial regulators, including the People’s Bank of China, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission, will hold meetings with major banks to study optimizing lending programs to support stock buybacks, Chinese media Cailian reported on Sunday.

Binance recorded a net outflow of $3.6 billion in crypto assets after restoring customer withdrawals on Sunday. The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said the flight of funds eased after an initial spike. Binance had frozen withdrawals following Thursday’s $6.3 billion hack while it investigated and stabilized the platform, and pledged to reimburse customers in full.

The dollar was mixed against its Group-of-10 peers on Monday, while US Treasuries edged lower as risks of deepening conflict in the Middle East fanned inflation concerns.

“Markets are placing significant weight on their expectations that US‑Iran fighting will escalate after the US midterm elections on 3 November,” Vivek Dhar, a strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, wrote in a note. “These concerns are justifiable given both the US and Iran believe they have the upper hand in the Middle East.”

Friday’s US stock slump delivered a long-awaited jolt of volatility after disappointing earnings from technology giants intensified concerns about the durability of the AI-driven rally.

The Cboe Volatility Index touched its highest intraday level since April, while demand for puts protecting against further losses surged and correlations among stocks climbed, signs of mounting stress. Still, those measures remain well below levels reached in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran.

The pullback is also prompting some investors to look for buying opportunities. Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson said he sees several “clearing events” ahead that could temporarily push stocks lower and create an opportunity for investors to add exposure.

“This looks more like a bullish rotation with a derating at its core than the beginning of a broad market deterioration,” said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Investment Management.

news.title: Trump's grip on Congress at stake as Americans vote in midterms on Tuesday
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 2 (IANS) Americans vote on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide whether President Donald Trump keeps a Republican-controlled Congress for the last two years of his term or faces a Democratic majority armed with subpoenas and control over spending. Republicans go into election day holding both chambers by thin margins. In the House of Representatives, Speaker Mike Johnson has 218 Republicans and one independent, Kevin Kiley of California, against 214 Democrats, with two seats vacant. "For Jeffries to get a chance to take the speaker's gavel, Democrats must attain a net gain of three seats, pushing their numbers to at least 218 -- a simple majority," ABC News reported. The Senate is split 53-47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to make Chuck Schumer majority leader, while Senate Majority Leader John Thune can lose three seats and keep control with Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote. Thirty-five Senate seats are on the ballot, 22 of them held by Republicans. The Cook Political Report rates seven Senate races as toss-ups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Six of those seats are held by Republicans and one by Democrats. "We see Democrats as the slight favorites," Cook said in its closing Senate analysis on October 30. In the House, Cook said, "we're projecting that Democrats flip 12 to 25 seats, giving them as many as 240 seats in the House." Sabato's Crystal Ball says Democrats appear to hold a narrow edge for the Senate. National polling points the same way. The RealClearPolling average of the generic congressional ballot on Sunday put Democrats ahead by about 51 per cent to 43 per cent, Newsweek reported, and the Silver Bulletin average shows a Democratic lead of about nine points. Trump's approval rating stands at about 37 per cent in the horserace.report average. The Silver Bulletin forecast gives Democrats about a 95 per cent chance of retaking the House and says that in the Senate, "Democrats do have a meaningful edge." The Economist's model gives Democrats a 55 per cent chance of flipping the Senate and about a 95 per cent chance in the House. History is against the President's party. Since 1946, presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their parties lose an average of 36 House seats in midterm elections, compared with 14 seats for presidents above that mark, according to Gallup. Republicans hope new maps will soften the blow. Ten states have redrawn their congressional maps since summer 2025, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Texas's new map could give Republicans up to five more seats, while California's voter-approved Proposition 50 makes five seats more favourable to Democrats, according to Ballotpedia Missouri's new map is on hold pending a referendum. For Trump, a Democratic House would mean investigations by committee chairs and leverage for Democrats over government funding, including money for the war with Iran. A Democratic Senate would also give Schumer's party control over the confirmation of judges and Cabinet nominees. For Democrats, the risk lies in the Senate map, which runs through states Trump won, some by double digits. Winning the House but falling short in the Senate would leave Republicans in charge of confirmations. Indian Americans are watching the results closely. At least 57 Indian American candidates are on Tuesday's ballot. Polls close in the first states at 6 p.m. Eastern time. Results in close races, including Alaska's ranked-choice count and California's slow count, could take days.

news.title: Middle East conflict: Trump threatens Iran with military action as Tehran warns new war could last longer
news.text:
President Donald Trump has been asking allies about the performances of War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, The Atlantic reported Sunday, citing two outside advisers close to him.

The questioning comes as Trump focuses on advisers who assured him the war would be "quick and decisive". He often seeks friends’ opinions before making personnel changes.

Some people close to Trump accused Hegseth of giving him an "overly optimistic" picture. The Pentagon rejected that claim, saying Hegseth provides the “full operational picture.” 

Hegseth and Caine presented military options to Trump and Vice President JD Vance at the White House last week, the report added.

The White House said Trump had “full confidence” in both men. No order to resume strikes had been given, the report said. 

The Atlantic noted that Trump has been contemplating a renewal of hostilities aimed at forcing Iran to negotiate. Advisers told the magazine that a new round of attacks could "come soon" after Tuesday’s midterms. 

Hegseth and Caine have been two of Trump’s key counselors on the war. In its earliest stages, they were among the most publicly optimistic about its prospects, though they have not held a press conference since May.

news.title: Cyber Attacks Hit Russia, Ukraine After Truce Ends
news.text: KYIV: Russia said its emergency warnings app came under a "massive cyberattack" on Monday, hours after Ukraine reported a hack in an apparent exchange of blows between the foes, as their longest truce came to an end. Moscow's emergencies ministry said hackers posted "false information" on the app, which is designed to warn the public of incoming drone attacks and other threats. Hours earlier, Ukraine said it suspected its air raid alert system had been compromised, after baseless alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the app. The cyber attacks came as the longest truce of the war, limited to Ukraine's eastern Kherson region, ended on Sunday after Russia refused the offer of an extension, according to Kyiv. Moscow did not immediately say who was behind the attack on its app, while Ukraine's Center for Strategic Communications SPRAVDI blamed the hack it suffered on Russia. The rare pause in fighting, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and which began early Tuesday, had enabled a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as the war grinds through its fifth year. "The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended," Ukraine's Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said. He called the temporary truce "an important step in our joint humanitarian efforts" with Russia. US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries -- as US counterpart Donald Trump has demanded -- if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles. - Raid alert app hack - Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin warned local people to be particularly vigilant when the ceasefire ended and to "respond immediately to warnings about Russian attacks". "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference," Ukraine's air force said in a message. "There is no radiation threat." Air force spokesman Yuriy Ignat confirmed to AFP that the app had been hacked. Hours later, Russia's emergencies ministry said its teams were working to fix a "massive cyberattack" which was "enabling attackers to send false information to the public". - 'Worse than before' - Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 has destroyed parts of eastern and southern Ukraine, left hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians dead and forced millions to flee their homes. AFP spoke to several Kherson residents, one of whom said the ceasefire had been a "breath of fresh air". "We have to use this time to get things done," said Volodymyr Omeltchenko, a 38-year-old gardener, before the truce ended. "We're pruning the rose bushes for winter." Pope Leo, who had pressed Russia for a truce in Oleshky, had said he hoped the temporary pause would "strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives". A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern that the fighting would be "worse than before" when it resumed. Russian forces on the other side of the Dnipro river had taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions using surveillance drones, the officer said. - Oil attacks - Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes elsewhere on Sunday. Russia said a drone had struck an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, with Ukrainian media reporting that Kyiv had attacked the Kstovo oil refinery. Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites, in what it says is fair retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump has been pressing Kyiv to stop the attacks, blaming them for rising diesel costs that analysts attribute to the Iran war. Zelensky said on Fox News on Sunday that he told Trump and his team: "If you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system." "Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles," he said. Ukraine's energy ministry reported fresh power outages across the country Sunday, including in Kyiv, following Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

news.title: Dollar rangebound ahead of US midterms; bitcoin reels from crypto heist
news.text:
SINGAPORE: The dollar and other major currencies were ​in a holding pattern on Monday as investors turned their attention to this week’s US midterm elections, which could ‌shift the balance of power in Congress and control over the federal purse strings.

In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin and ether were nursing losses following last week’s record $6.3 billion heist at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange.

Traders were bracing for a packed week dominated by the US midterm elections, October US jobs data and ​central bank rate decisions in the UK, Australia, Norway and Sweden.

Ahead of the week’s events, the euro languished near a ​17-month low at $1.1159 in early Asian trade, weighed down by Fitch’s revision of France’s outlook to “negative” from “stable” ⁠after Friday’s close.

Sterling was little changed at $1.3387, while the dollar steadied at 101.94 against a basket of currencies.

Americans head to the ​polls on Tuesday to determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

Democrats are widely predicted ​to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is more in doubt.

“The challenge we face in analysing election outcomes is that polling suggests strong anti-incumbent sentiment, but that does not always translate into actual election outcomes - as we have seen in Brazil and now in Israel,” said Eric Robertsen, ​global head of research and chief strategist at Standard Chartered.

In the event of a Democratic sweep of Congress, Robertsen said capex ​plans for data centres and AI infrastructure could face increasing obstacles at the state level, while the next debate on raising the US debt ‌ceiling would ⁠be among the most contentious in recent history.

Meanwhile, Andreja Cobeljic, head of derivatives trading at AMINA Bank, said hedge funds had suffered “significant losses” in October, leaving markets with “little capacity” to absorb any surprises from the midterm elections.

In other currencies, the yen eased 0.15% to 157.78 per dollar.

The Australian dollar was flat at $0.7033 ahead of Tuesday’s policy decision, where the Reserve Bank of Australia is widely ​expected to raise its cash ​rate to a near two-decade ⁠high of 4.85%.

The New Zealand dollar fell 0.11% to $0.5625, having slid 1.2% last week in the wake of its central bank’s surprise decision to leave rates unchanged.

Elsewhere, bitcoin was up 0.22% at $77,975.62, having fallen ​to a six-week low on Friday. Ether was up 0.27% to $2,268.42, having similarly slid to ​a two-month trough ⁠last week.

Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the exchange went back online on Sunday after hackers the FBI links to North Korea stole billions from the platform last week.

Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. The ⁠exchange ​said it had now covered 95% of the $6.3 billion of stolen assets.

“The crypto ​industry has spent a decade making blockchains mathematically secure. It still runs on the assumption that an employee’s laptop can be trusted,” said Richard Forss, chief technology ​officer at global prime broker EXANTE.

“That assumption is now the weakest point in digital finance.”

"We're pruning the rose bushes for winter."Pope Leo, who had pressed Russia for a truce in Oleshky, said he hoped the temporary pause would "strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives".A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern that the fighting would be "worse than before" when it resumed.Russian forces on the other side of the Dnipro river, had taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks, and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions using surveillance drones, the officer said.Refinery Reportedly HitRussia and Ukraine exchanged strikes elsewhere on Sunday.Russia said early Sunday that a drone had struck an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight.Ukrainian media reported that Kyiv had attacked the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it "one of Russia's largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants".Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites, in what it says is fair retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.Trump has been pressing Kyiv to stop such attacks, blaming them for rising diesel costs that analysts attribute to the Iran war.On Sunday, Zelensky referred to conversations he had had with Trump and his team on the issue, in an interview with Fox News."We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid," said Zelensky.Ukraine's energy ministry reported fresh power outages across the country Sunday, including in Kyiv, following Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.Ukrainian strikes killed five people in Russian-occupied Ukraine between late Saturday and Sunday afternoon, Russian-installed authorities said.Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians.Russia now occupies around a fifth of its neighbour: the Crimean peninsula, which it annexed in 2014, most of the eastern regions of Donetsk and Lugansk -- collectively referred to as the Donbas -- and large parts of the southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern that the fighting would be "worse than before" when it resumed.
