news.title: Binance sees outflows stabilising as exchange returns online after $6.3 billion heist
news.text: Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion stolen from the platform last week.The exchange moved to reassure crypto investors and said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial". It said it had now covered 95% of the assets stolen in the heist.After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered slightly through the weekend to trade above $78,000 on Monday. Ether hit a two-month low on Friday and also recovered a little to $2,287.Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally. It said on Sunday it had $171 billion in total assets under management as of October 28."(That) puts the withdrawals in the range of a precautionary reaction rather than any sort of capital flight," said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs.The Binance theft, which analysts say could be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust Binance with their money after the attack.Stablecoin market capitalisations tend to fall when money is leaving cryptocurrencies and they have dropped since Friday. The combined capitalisation of the two largest stablecoins, USDT and USDC, has dropped by about $1.2 billion since Friday, according to Coinmarketcap.com.PHASED WITHDRAWALSBinance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in stages, prioritising user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin."We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand," Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.It added, "Rest assured that market conditions are stable."Binance said earlier on Sunday it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of less liquid assets and may take longer to source in the required amounts, it said.Binance said the net outflows reflected what clients had withdrawn and deposited after the event. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $5.81 billion, up from the $4.36 billion it showed earlier. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the updated figures."This figure does not contain the flows we have deposited to our own new hot wallet, so they are not accurate. Our last update on X is closest to accurate (outstanding the moves in both deposits and withdrawals since it was posted)," a spokesperson for Binance said of the initial DefiLlama data.FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNITThe FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.Analysts had also pointed to North Korea's involvement. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.US President Donald Trump, however, later on Saturday said it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved."We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters in comments posted by a White House account on X.BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTSBinance said it will bear the financial impact of the hack and has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses.The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance's $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.Co-CEO Yi He said on the weekend Binance would use 50% of its SAFU funds, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 billion. She warned Binance had been made aware of new scams that had emerged during the past few days "amid the chaos".
news.summary: Binance customers pulled $3.64 billion, or 2.1% of its assets, as the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange resumed service after a security breach linked to North Korea saw $6.3 billion stolen from the platform last week.

news.title: Leak Reveals Trump Secretly Doubting Pentagon Pete
news.text:
Several White House insiders have revealed cracks in President Donald Trump’s relationship with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

Citing two outside advisers close to Trump, new reporting in The Atlantic reveals the president has begun questioning a group of close allies over Hegseth’s performance as head of the Department of Defense, and is even considering using the 46-year-old as a scapegoat for the flailing war effort in Iran.

The advisers, and other unidentified figures close to Trump, said they believe these conversations are possibly a prelude to Hegseth’s firing, based on Trump’s past behavior when making changes to his Cabinet, according to the report.

“Hegseth is good at telling the president what he wants to hear,” one of the outside advisers told the Atlantic.

He has also been soliciting opinions on Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman, Gen. Dan Caine, according to the sources. 

Hegseth and Caine have led the effort to advise Trump throughout the war. Hegseth, in particular, has been the public face of the conflict, consistently reasserting that Iran was pursuing nuclear arms before the war began. 

Trump is currently weighing whether he should renew strikes on Iran after the midterms, receiving detailed options for campaigns from Hegseth and Caine that range from days to weeks of additional strikes–as well as an option to cease the conflict entirely, the Atlantic reports, adding that he has not yet given any orders to resume strikes. 

The two advisers and an official said Trump has fumed in recent weeks and credits the war with his political troubles. 

The White House and the Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment. 

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told the Atlantic, “President Trump and everyone at the White House have full confidence in both Secretary Hegseth and General Caine, who are fully aligned with the President’s mission.”

Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesperson, added in a separate statement to the Atlantic that “Secretary Hegseth always provides the President and White House senior leaders the full operational picture.” 

Parnell added that Hegseth was committed to “promoting the right senior military officers to leadership positions and retiring those who are unwilling to effectively serve the only person in government elected by the whole of the American people: President Donald J. Trump.” 

Hegseth, a former Fox News pundit, has described the conflict to Trump in purely positive terms, without accurately briefing the president about the situation on the ground, sources told the Atlantic. Hegseth was one of the main proponents of the early theory that the Iran war would only last four to six weeks. 

But as the war approaches its ninth month, Trump has been reconsidering the effectiveness of Hegseth’s military leadership. In a gesture of good will, Hegseth has purged nearly two dozen top generals in the military for a range of petty offenses that displease the president; most recently, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, for his alleged leaks to the press. 

Hegseth has previously faced calls for impeachment from both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis have each publicly called for his removal since September.

news.title: Plane crash near Trump's Mar-a-Lago kills nine as pilot warned 'we're going to crash'
news.text: Nine people have died after a private jet crash close to a mobile home park, merely six miles from Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago residence. The Learjet 60 plummeted into a residential neighbourhood in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, at approximately 12.50pm EST (5.50pm GMT) on Sunday, officials confirmed. Reports suggest it struck a tree and knocked down electricity cables during the incident. The aircraft had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was travelling towards North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. The plane vanished from flight-tracking systems after dropping roughly 27,000ft within the span of a minute. Officials have not yet established the cause behind the aircraft's descent, however, distressing audio from the plane revealed the final moments experienced by those aboard. The jet was travelling eastbound at 35,000 feet when crew members reported turbulence, ice formation and bad weather conditions. The pilot declared an emergency situation as the plane started losing height at a worrying speed, reports the Express . "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot communicated via radio, before delivering a heartbreaking realisation of their fate. "We're going to crash into the ground." Jim Reynolds, a representative for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, was unable to immediately share information regarding the passengers on the flight. "This is definitely a tragedy," Mr Reynolds commented. Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed the incident, stating: "An incident involving an aircraft is currently under investigation in the area of Military Trail, between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North." Roads in both directions were shut down by the sheriff's office, with motorists urged to steer clear of the area . The Learjet 60, a mid-size business jet, typically carries six to seven passengers along with two crew members. Flight tracking service Flightradar24 revealed the jet had taken off from Austin, Texas, bound for the Bahamas, reaching a cruising altitude of 41,000 feet. "At 17:35, near Naples, FL, the aircraft began a descent to 35,000 feet. At 17:48, the aircraft briefly climbed before entering a steep, right-hand descent," Flightradar24 added. Shocking dashcam footage captured the horrifying moment the jet nosedived into the tarmac before erupting into a massive fireball, with flames and thick black smoke billowing from the wreckage. Stunned locals gathered at the scene, with witnesses telling local outlet Boca News Now the impact sounded like a missile strike. Both the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) have launched investigations into the crash, with the NTSB taking the lead, according to the FAA. This marks the second deadliest aviation disaster in the US this year, following a skydiving plane crash in Butler, Missouri, in June, which claimed all 12 lives on board.
news.summary: A private jet carrying nine people has crashed near Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, with audio capturing the final moments of those onboard as the Learjet 60 plummeted to the ground in Greenacres, Palm Beach County
news.author: Antonio Scancariello,Tannur Anders

news.title: Nuclear scare, fake radiation warnings: Cyberattacks hit Russia, Ukraine alert systems
news.text: Ukraine and Russia have reported cyberattacks targeting their emergency alert systems, with hackers allegedly circulating fake warnings of radiation, chemical and nuclear threats, raising concerns over the disruption of public safety communications amid the ongoing war between the two countries.Ukraine's air raid alert application was reportedly compromised on Sunday, sending false warnings about chemical and radiation threats to mobile phones across the country. Loudspeaker systems in Kyiv also broadcast similar messages, prompting the Ukrainian Air Force to warn of possible external interference."Attention. The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," the Air Force said on Telegram, adding that, "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!"Ukraine's Central Intelligence Agency also reported a failure in the application and urged residents to consult alternative sources of information to verify warnings about possible air strikes.Also Read:'Maximum deterrence': Mojtaba Khamenei meets top generals, issues warning to USHowever, the Ministry of Digital Transformation later said the nationwide alert system was functioning normally."The nationwide alert system is operating in normal mode. All threat signals are transmitted to regional administrations and, accordingly, to street alert systems," the ministry said in a post on X.Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations said its mobile application had been targeted in a massive cyberattack that enabled attackers to distribute false public safety information. Russian authorities also reported fake warnings about nuclear strikes inside the country, with a Ukrainian espionage group reportedly suspected of involvement."The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app was subjected to a massive cyberattack, which allowed the attackers to distribute fake information to the public," the ministry said in a statement.According to TASS, the ministry said efforts were underway to eliminate the vulnerability in the application and restore its normal functioning.Also Read: Russia arrests minor after US tip-off on terror plot targeting MoscowThe incidents come amid continuing military operations and diplomatic efforts surrounding the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The false alerts in Ukraine were reportedly circulated shortly before the end of a localised ceasefire in the Oleshky area of Ukraine's Kherson region.On Sunday, US First Lady Melania Trump commended Moscow and Kyiv for their cooperation during the five-day humanitarian ceasefire, which concluded on November 1. news.title: Trump says he may become ‘Mr. Veto’ if Democrats win US midterm elections
news.text:
President Donald Trump said he may have to become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats win a majority in Tuesday’s midterms, according to a clip of a New York Post interview aired Sunday on Fox News.

“They’ll be sending stuff up, you veto it,” he said in the preview clip of the New York Post podcast interview aired on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures ahead of its release Monday. “Eventually, after a month or two of getting all vetoed — you know, it’s just waste — they come over and make a deal.”

It marks a rare acknowledgment by Trump that his party may lose the midterm elections, even as he heads Sunday to Kansas and Iowa to hold more rallies. The president has been campaigning nonstop, traveling to states that have traditionally been GOP strongholds but where the party faces a tougher path amid voter anxiety over the high cost of living and the war in Iran.

Most polls show Democrats well positioned to pick up the three House seats they need to win control of the chamber, and they are growing more confident about being able to take the Senate, with seven races polling within a narrow margin.

“Hopefully we don’t have to worry about that,” Trump said in the clip. 

Republican strategists say their private data paints a more competitive Senate picture, with many of the key races still toss-ups or within reach. In his speeches, Trump has stuck with his rhetoric that the country has the “greatest economy in history” and that polls don’t show Republican votes correctly.

In another clip from the interview, Trump said that he would “love to run again if I had the chance, but the language is very exacting,” referring to the Constitution.

The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution forbids a commander-in-chief from being elected to more than two terms.

news.summary: The President’s remarks come as Republicans face a challenging election campaign amid voter concerns over living costs and the Iran war

news.title: Plane crash near Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago in Florida kills nine people
news.text: Nine people have died after a private aircraft plummeted near a mobile home park, merely six miles from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence. The Learjet 60 crashed in a residential neighbourhood in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, at approximately 12.50pm EST (5.50pm GMT) on Sunday, officials confirmed. It allegedly struck a tree and knocked down electricity cables in the incident. The jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was travelling to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. It then vanished from flight-tracking platforms after dropping roughly 27,000ft within the span of a minute. Officials did not straight away verify what led to the aircraft going down, but distressing audio from the jet recorded the final moments of those aboard. The aircraft was travelling eastbound at 35,000 feet when pilots encountered turbulence, icing and precipitation. The pilot declared an emergency as the jet started losing height at a worrying speed. "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot communicated via radio, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground." Jim Reynolds, a representative for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, could not immediately provide details about who was onboard. "This is definitely a tragedy," Mr Reynolds said. Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office confirmed the crash, stating: "An incident involving an aircraft is currently under investigation in the area of Military Trail, between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North." The sheriff's office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. The Learjet 60 is a mid-size business jet that typically accommodates six to seven passengers, alongside two crew members. According to Flightradar24, the jet departed Austin, Texas, bound for the Bahamas, climbing to a cruising altitude of 41,000 feet. "At 17:35, near Naples, FL, the aircraft began a descent to 35,000 feet. At 17:48, the aircraft briefly climbed before entering a steep, right-hand descent," Flightradar24 added. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are jointly investigating the crash, with the NTSB taking the lead, according to the FAA. news.title: Ukrainian air raid alert app sends false warnings after being hacked
news.text:
Ukraine's air force says the country's public air raid alert app has been hacked.

For a short time the app showed false warnings that Kyiv and other areas faced nuclear, chemical and street combat threats.

"The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence," the Ukrainian air force said on Telegram. 

"There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!"

The announcement came minutes after the end of the truce between Moscow and Kyiv in the eastern region of Kherson. 

The localised ceasefire on Tuesday, which was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, was the longest of the war.

In a post on its X account, Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications (SPRAVDI) blamed Russia for the hack.

The app is used across Ukraine to warn people in real time about air strikes from Russia. 

People often have only minutes to find shelter in the case of, for example, a ballistic missile attack.

"Currently, the information broadcast [on this application] about threat levels does not correspond to reality," the Ukrainian Centre for Countering Disinformation warned in a statement.

Ukraine's digital transformation ministry said the app was not operating, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as were air raid sirens.

Russian emergencies ministry's mobile app hit by cyber attack

Russia's emergencies ministry mobile app was also hit by a massive cyber attack, state news agency TASS quoted the ministry as saying. 

It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.

The ministry was working to restore the app, TASS said, without providing additional details.

Russia's emergencies ministry said the application was designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday, local time, his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries — as US counterpart Donald Trump had demanded — if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.

Reuters/AFP
news.summary: The app has sent Ukrainians false warnings that some areas of the country face nuclear and chemical threats.

news.title: Fact-checking El-Sayed and Rogers on 60 Minutes
news.text: With 48 hours to go before polls close in Michigan, few midterm races in the country have captured as much attention as the contest playing out between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.Rogers is seeking to become Michigan's first Republican U.S. senator in 25 years, as Democrats try to hold onto the seat. The contest has become increasingly tense in recent days, with El-Sayed engaged in a public rift with his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, who he beat by fewer than 15,000 votes.In a stunning turn, Stevens, who had been expected to appear alongside El-Sayed at a campaign event, instead appeared with Rogers Sunday at a Detroit church service – and endorsed him for Senate. "I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted Sunday on social media. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, called Stevens' move a "despicable betrayal."It was only the latest turn in a hotly contested, closely watched race, which is why we led tonight's 60 Minutes broadcast with this story. Correspondent Ross Douthat sat down with both candidates as they made their cases to Michigan voters: on the economy, healthcare, Israel and other issues that have come to define the race.The contest is close and contentious. On the campaign trail, President Trump has been throwing his support behind Rogers and disparaging El-Sayed as a "jihadist."Along with the broadcast segment, we decided to post extended interviews with El-Sayed and Rogers. We're doing so for a simple reason: these conversations are in the public interest. And we owe our viewers as much transparency as possible—especially in a race of such consequence.60 Minutes sat down with each candidate for more than an hour in late October. In their interviews, both candidates made several claims that were false, misleading or unsupported by our reporting. We believe it is important to share those claims and provide the facts and context viewers need to evaluate them:Rogers claims El-Sayed wrote a letter supporting Muslim BrotherhoodRogers claimed that El-Sayed "wrote a letter in support for the Muslim Brotherhood … when they took over Egypt in 20 — whatever that was, 2012 and 2013 — that I think is very, very concerning. And, again, it's not about how he prays. It is his ideology. It's the way he thinks."Our reporting shows that after the Arab Spring, El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian-Americans who signed a letter addressed to Egypt's new democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, who was a senior leader of the Muslim Brotherhood. The letter urged Morsi to take action against allies of the country's previous authoritarian leader. At the time, the United States had not designated the organization as a terrorist group. Earlier this year, the Trump administration called branches of the organization terrorist entities.El-Sayed denies any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and has publicly disavowed the group. El-Sayed claims Michigan utility DTE "buys off almost every politician in our state"When asked to give an example of a monopoly that has held power over an extended period of time, El-Sayed named DTE, saying, "They have raised our rates faster than in 46 other states over the past 20 years. They buy off almost every politician in our state, so that, you know, they all look the other way and they just make money hand over fist."DTE and its political action committee have made extensive, publicly reported contributions to Michigan politicians, including a large majority of state legislators, but 60 Minutes found no evidence that DTE made improper payments in exchange for votes or regulatory decisions. El-Sayed claims Rogers "made 14 million bucks" after leaving CongressEl-Sayed said "the rules of our game in politics are about taking corporate money to do corporate bidding and then make money on the back end of the same corporations you're regulating" and suggested his opponent has "played that game.""He made 14 million bucks and moved to Florida, bought a mansion and two yachts, and he's watching Donald Trump play that game and make billions," El-Sayed claimed.Financial disclosures show Rogers' household net worth rose substantially after he left office in 2015, to an estimated $7 million to $14 million or more, but those figures reflect net worth, not earnings, and 60 Minutes was unable to verify that Rogers made $14 million. As for the yachts, Rogers registered two boats in Maryland (32 feet and 39 feet, respectively) and sold one before registering the other.Rogers calls El-Sayed a Democratic socialistRogers called his opponent "a very gifted Democrat Socialist of America." While El-Sayed has campaigned with some prominent Democratic socialists, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, nor has the group officially endorsed him.When Douthat asked El-Sayed, "Were you ever a socialist," the candidate responded: "No. I'm a capitalist." Rogers says El-Sayed wants to defund the policeWhile expounding on El-Sayed as a Democratic socialist, Rogers said: "If you look at his issue set, defund the police, let people out of prison, all of the things that are associated with that Democrat socialist, big government — government taking over private health care, you lose your private health insurance, that's all DSA."It's true that El-Sayed called for defunding the police back in 2020 following the killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis. El-Sayed recently called it "a pretty dumb and unnuanced slogan" but said "that was the conversation that was happening." Most recently while campaigning for the Senate, El-Sayed has called for increased funding for police recruitment, retention and retirement.Watch: Extended interview with El-SayedWatch: Extended interview with Rogers
news.summary: Ross Douthat sat down with both candidates as they made their cases to Michigan voters.

news.title: Trump administration promises US farmers $15B in the weeks before the midterms
news.text: SIOUX FALLS — President Donald Trump's administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks before the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran.Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election.A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers:Whom these efforts will helpBesides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice.Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines.Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to 'more than cover the increase in fuel costs,' and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices.At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects.On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs.The money will primarily come from the USDA and doesn't need immediate congressional approval.The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock.Why farmers are strugglingIt has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods.On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 perWhat farmers may vote on gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago.'That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what's going to happen in the world,' Ibendahl said.He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices.'It's hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, 'OK, well, we're looking pretty good this year, but it's all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?'' he said.Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution.What farmers may vote onRural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump.Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products.'Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man,' he said. 'But it doesn't mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn't on the ballot this year. His policies are.'Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy.Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates.'Independent voters make or break elections,' she said. 'And so that's really what it's going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they're breaking for.

news.title: Trump Reacts to Murphy Stroke Days After Senator's 'Insane' Iran Warning
news.text: President Donald Trump reacted to news that Democratic Senator Chris Murphy suffered a stroke, days after he called a possible administration plan for renewed military action against Iran “insane.” After landing in Dubuque, Iowa, for a campaign rally, Trump told reporters on Sunday that he was “really surprised” to learn about the Connecticut senator's stroke. "Nobody wants to have that,” he added. Murphy, 53, began experiencing numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game Saturday afternoon, his chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement. “He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” Herwitt said. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment.” Doctors were encouraged by Murphy’s progress, and he was awake and alert, Herwitt added. “We are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” she said. Murphy serves on the Senate's Appropriations and Foreign Relations committees and is a leading voice on immigration and gun policy. He is considered a contender for more senior leadership positions in the chamber and among the many Democrats seen as potential 2028 candidates for the White House. Murphy Called Possible Iran Plan ‘Insane’ Murphy said last week that he had been briefed on a possible resumption of U.S. military operations against Iran. The Democrat discussed the briefing during a Middle East Institute event in Washington following a trip to Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He said lawmakers had received a detailed description of what a renewed military campaign could look like. Asked about the proposal, Murphy said: “Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation, and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.” Murphy said officials had been asked by Trump to develop a plan, although he said he did not know whether they believed it would work. “The plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests,” Murphy said. Murphy also addressed the issue on social media on October 29. “Trump is reportedly planning to restart war with Iran after the election,” he wrote. “Some of us have been briefed on the war plan. And while I cannot disclose any details, I can say this: the plan is insane.” He added that the plan “will not achieve objectives and will set off a new cycle of escalation.” According to the Wall Street Journal, the White House recently briefed allies in the Middle East to prepare for a "short, intense military campaign" against Iran as soon as November 4, the day after the midterm elections, according to three senior Gulf Arab officials, granted anonymity to share sensitive discussions. Trump said Friday that the Iran war “is going to be over very soon.” Newsweek reached out to the White House and Pentagon for comment on Sunday. Murphy Was Campaigning Ahead of Midterms Murphy is not on the ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections but had been traveling in support of Democratic candidates as the party battles to regain control of Congress. He had recently campaigned in Connecticut for Governor Ned Lamont and in Minnesota with Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic Senate nominee. Lawmakers from both parties offered messages of support following news of his stroke. Senator John Fetterman, a Pennsylvania Democrat, who suffered a stroke while campaigning for the Senate in 2022, said his family “is rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery.” Several other Democratic senators have suffered strokes in recent years. Senators Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland had strokes in 2022 and recovered. Connecticut Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal described Murphy as a “great friend & colleague.” “I know how fiercely he fights & I’m certain I’ll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon,” he said. Republican Senators Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska also offered prayers for Murphy. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Steven Frank.
news.summary: Trump reacted to the Democratic senator's stroke days after he called a possible administration plan for Iran “insane.”
